summary: Describes RC2, a secret-key block encryption algorithm, that was offered as a possible replacement for DES. It is informational and documents the algorithm rather than endorsing it.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a recipe for scrambling messages with a secret key. It was written down so others could use it.

subtitle: A variable-key-size, 64-bit block cipher designed to run quickly on 16-bit microprocessors.

tldr.problem: A secret-key block cipher was wanted that could be a proposal for a DES replacement and that is easy to implement on 16-bit microprocessors.
tldr.mechanism: RC2 expands a key of 1 to 128 bytes into 64 sixteen-bit words, then runs a 64-bit block through 16 mixing rounds and 2 mashing rounds that use those words.
tldr.outcome: The memo documents the algorithm with test vectors and an object identifier for RC2 in CBC mode. It is Informational and does not endorse RC2 as a standard.

today: RFC 2268 is an Informational memo from March 1998 and is not obsoleted or updated by any other RFC. It documents the RC2 algorithm and does not specify an Internet standard.

sections.title: What RC2 Is
sections.content:
This memo, an RSA Laboratories Technical Note, describes RC2, a conventional secret-key block cipher that may be considered a proposal for a DES replacement. Input and output blocks are 64 bits each. The key size is variable, from one byte up to 128 bytes, although the current implementation uses eight bytes.

The algorithm is designed to be easy to implement on 16-bit microprocessors. On an IBM AT, the memo says encryption runs about twice as fast as DES, assuming key expansion has been done.

Three algorithms are involved: key expansion, encryption and decryption. A 'word' is a 16-bit quantity.
sections.plainLanguage: RC2 chops a message into small pieces and scrambles each one with a secret key. It was built to be quick on small, old computers.

sections.title: Key Expansion
sections.content:
The supplied key of T bytes (1 to 128) is placed in a 128-byte buffer L, which can also be viewed as 64 sixteen-bit words K[0] to K[63]. The goal is that each bit of the expanded key depends in a complicated way on every bit of the supplied key.

The algorithm also has a maximum effective key length in bits, T1. The search space is 2^(8*T) or 2^T1, whichever is smaller. Two loops fill the rest of the buffer using PITABLE, a 256-byte permutation of the values 0 to 255 based on the digits of pi, and a mask on one byte limits the effective bits to T1. For example, with T1 = 64 the mask TM is 0xff, and with T1 = 63 it is 0x7f.

The expanded key is not changed during encryption or decryption, so it can be expanded once for a large amount of data.
sections.plainLanguage: Before scrambling, RC2 stretches your short secret into a long list of numbers by mixing it with a fixed table, so every number depends on the whole secret.

sections.title: Encryption
sections.content:
The 64-bit block is held in four words R[0] to R[3]. Encryption is built from two primitives. A mix step adds the next unused key word and a combination of the neighbouring words to R[i], then rotates it left by 1, 2, 3 or 5 bits depending on i. A mash step adds to R[i] the key word chosen by the low six bits of R[i-1].

A mixing round does a mix on each of the four words, and a mashing round does a mash on each. The full operation is: five mixing rounds, one mashing round, six mixing rounds, one mashing round, five mixing rounds. That is 16 mixing rounds, so each key word is used exactly once in a mix, while the mashing rounds refer to key words in a data-dependent way.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of four people passing notes. Each round, each person adds a number from the key list to their note and shifts it around, depending on what their neighbour holds.

sections.title: Decryption
sections.content:
Decryption undoes encryption step by step using r-mix and r-mash primitives. R-mix rotates right and then subtracts the key word and the neighbour-based word, and the key index counts down from 63. R-mash subtracts the key word selected by the low six bits of R[i-1].

The overall order mirrors encryption: five r-mixing rounds, one r-mashing round, six r-mixing rounds, one r-mashing round and five r-mixing rounds, with the words processed from R[3] down to R[0] in each round.
sections.plainLanguage: To unscramble, you do every step in reverse order, subtracting what was added and rotating the other way.

sections.title: Test Vectors and the CBC Identifier
sections.content:
The memo lists eight test vectors, with key lengths from 1 to 33 bytes and effective key lengths from 63 to 129 bits, so implementers can check their code. For example, an eight-byte all-zero key with 63 effective bits turns an all-zero plaintext block into ebb773f9 93278eff.

It also defines the object identifier rc2CBC for RC2 in cipher block chaining mode. The parameters are either a simple 8-octet IV or a sequence of a version number and an IV. The version number, 1 to 1024, encodes the effective key bits: for 1 to 255 bits it is looked up in a 256-byte table, and for 256 to 1024 it equals the bit count. The default is 32 effective key bits, in which case only the IV should be supplied.

An appendix notes that RC2 is a registered trademark of RSA Data Security, Inc., and that RSA's copyrighted RC2 software is available under license.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo includes answer keys so you can check your recipe works, and a label saying how to tell others which key size and starting value you used.
